verdict.reasoning: Patient states symptoms began “about two to three days ago” and describes being unable to talk while running due to shortness of breath: “about two to three days ago I was running with a friend and usually I could talk to her whilst I ran, but I found myself actually short of breath… definitely if I'm walking briskly now.”
Patient reports “I'm just wheezing a bit and coughing” and denies sputum: “Are you bringing up any phlegm at all? … No, I don't. I'm not coughing up much sputum.”

Patient says they use the blue inhaler “as and when I have symptoms” and confirms current use “every day at the moment… and morning and evening to kind of prevent it as well,” but later clarifies “the salbutamol is just like as and when.” Thus it is used as needed, not consistently morning and evening as a standing regimen.
Use: “How are you using the Klenol? Is it twice a day? – Yes.” Advice: “If you're using just two puffs twice a day, you can increase it to four puffs twice a day.”
When asked, “have you ever been admitted in hospital because your asthma was so bad?” the patient replies, “No, I haven't,” indicating no hospitalizations for asthma.
“When was the last time you had an asthma attack? – About three to four years ago.”
“When was the last time you had an asthma review with our nurse? – About two years ago.”
“Have you ever had oral steroids in the past? – No.”

Monitoring: “So do you do a peak flow meter at home? … No. – Just every now and then. I haven't done over the last. Since I've had symptoms.” Usual value: “what's your peak flow reading then? … I think 130. – Okay. Let's say it's about 380. … so that's your normal.” The summary “about 380” matches the agreed usual value.
Allergy history: “Do you have any allergies at all? – I have hay fever… Sorry, I have hay fever.”
Patient indicates possible eczema: “my sister has eczema and I've got a few issues that I think could be eczema as well.”

The fact states daily morning and evening use plus PRN. Transcript: early, “Yeah, and morning and evening to kind of prevent it as well,” but later clarifies “the salbutamol is just like as and when.” Overall, it is used PRN (and currently frequently), not prescribed as a fixed morning-and-evening preventer regimen.
“How are you using your, your Kleno? So are you using it every day? – I think I'm using that every day.” and “So how are you using the Klenol? Is it twice a day? – Yes.”
After hay fever is mentioned, clinician asks: “any med. Allergies to medication? – Oh, no, sorry. – Okay, so you're not allergic to anything. Okay, so no allergies.”
Family history: “My brother's asthmatic and my sister has eczema.”
Same line: “My brother's asthmatic and my sister has eczema.”
Peak flow monitoring: “I haven't done over the last. Since I've had symptoms,” confirming it has not been measured since onset of current symptoms.

Duration and symptoms: “about two to three days ago… short of breath… I'm just wheezing a bit and coughing… I've used my blue inhaler, but to no avail. It hasn't really helped me.” Clinician assessment: “it looks like you can be having a small, small exacerbation.” This supports a mild ongoing exacerbation with increased SOB, wheeze, cough despite inhaler use over 2–3 days.

“The brown inhaler, you can up the dose. If you're using just two puffs twice a day, you can increase it to four puffs twice a day… By increasing your clinical, we are increasing your steroid intake.”

“You can use your blue inhaler as and when. Okay. Use it maximum about every two to four hours. But if you're using it that often, that means too much… you can use it, but that's not ideal.” This aligns with use every 2–4 hours PRN, with heavy use indicating need for further care.

“I would like you to be seen by one of our GPS in the next few days… I will recommend that you need a face to face.” and “when the doctor sees you, what we're going to do is we're going to examine your chest… Make you do the peak reading.” This is an urgent face-to-face GP review with chest exam and peak flow.
“Depending on what we find, you might need some antibiotics or some steroids.” This is conditional consideration of escalation to oral steroids or antibiotics.

Warning signs and ED advice: “if you're using [blue inhaler] that often, that means too much… and your breathing's getting really worse. Then you would need to take yourself to A. E. You shouldn't wait for our appointment.” This is education on red flags requiring emergency care.
Follow-up: “I would like you to be seen by one of our GPS in the next few days… I will recommend that you need a face to face.” indicates a planned urgent face-to-face GP review.
